senses.gloss:
Madhubrāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
The fifth ब्राह्मण or section of the second chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad is called Madhubrāhmaṇa because the word ‘madhu’ has been used frequently (34 times).
‘Madhu’ means honey. Since honey is a कार्य or effect produced by the honey-bees, and, being sweet and enjoyable, is liked by everybody, anything that is liked by people can be compared to मधु or honey.
Since the five elements—earth, water, fire, air and space or ether—as also other items of nature in च्रेअतिओन् like the sun, the मोओन्, the lightning are effects and are necessary for our existence and sustenance, they are compared to मधु or honey.
It is interesting to note that the Upaniṣad has included धर्म (righteousness), सत्य (truth), mānuṣa (humankind) as also the आत्मन् in the list of madhus.

madhumatī
(‘that which contains [the word] मधु’)
------------------------------------------
Offering madhuparka—a liquid preparation containing a mixture of curds, ghee, water, honey and sugar—to the ṛtviks or priests in a Vedic sacrifice is an important way of honouring them. These ṛtviks are expected to sanctify it by looking at it and repeating the three ṛks or verses starting with ‘madhu vātā ṛtāyate’ and ending with ‘mādhvīr gāvo bhavantu naḥ’ (Ṛgveda 1.90.6-8). Since all the three verses begin with the word ‘madhu’ they are together called ‘madhumatī’ verses.
This repetition brings auspiciousness on the yajamāna or the sacrificer.
This procedure is mentioned in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtras (1.24.5-26) as also in the Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtras (1.3).

Mādhyandina-śākhā
(‘the recension [edited by the sage] Madhyandina’)
------------------------------------------
The sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana—more well-known as व्यास or Vedavyāsa—took the trouble of collecting all the Vedic mantras available during his time and edited them, dividing them into four groups or sections to suit the smooth conduct of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. He then taught these four to his four chief disciples: पैल, वैशम्पायन, जैमिनि and सुमन्तु. The वेदस् they received came to be known respectively, as Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda and Atharvaveda.
Yājñavalkya, the most brilliant of the students of वैशम्पायन, separated from him due to serious differences of opinion and got a different version of the Yajurveda directly from the Sun-god who taught him assuming the हयग्रीव form (human frame with a horse’s head). This Veda came to be known as Śukla Yajurveda. He taught it to his fifteen disciples of whom the sages कण्व and Madhyandina were, perhaps, more prominent.
When these two disciples re-edited the Śukla Yajurveda, it got bifurcated into two शाखास् or branches which came to be known by their names, viz., the Kāṇva-śākhā and the Mādhyandinaśākhā.
The Mādhyandinaśākhā or recension is more popular in North India and the Kāṇva in the South. It has 40 adhyāyas or chapters and 1975 mantras. It is smaller than the Kāṇva recension.
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad is found in both the recensions.
There are no major differences between these two recensions.
See ŚATAPATHABRĀHMAṆA and ŚUKLA-YAJURVEDA also.

Madhucchandas
------------------------------------------
Every मन्त्र or ṛk of the Ṛgveda is attributed to some ṛṣi or sage. He is the person through whom the मन्त्र was revealed.
Madhucchandas, one of the sons of the famous sage विश्वामित्र, is the ṛṣi of the first ten sūktas of the first मण्डल of the Ṛgveda. The total number of mantras or ṛks in these ten sūktas is 102.
He has also been mentioned in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (28.2) and the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (1.1.3).
The ṛṣis to whom a hundred or more ṛks were revealed, came to be known as Śatarcins. मधुच्छन्दस् is ranked first among them.

madhubhūmika
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) warns the योगि that he must not succumb to the temptations of sthānis—those occupying celestial worlds like Indra—and should not also fall a prey to egoism, in the process of rejecting their offers (vide 3.51).
The commentator व्यास (A. D. 600) divides the yogis into four categories out of which the मधुभूमिक (yogi) is the second. He is the one who has attained ऋतम्भरप्रज्ञा (vide Vyāsabhāṣya on the Yogasūtras 1.48), and therefore is capable of straightforward and truthful perception. The advice in the sūtra 51 is meant for him.

Madhuvidyā
------------------------------------------
See CHĀNDOGYA UPANIṢAD, UPANIṢADS and VIDYĀS.

Madhyadeśa
(‘the middle part of the country [Bhāratavarṣa]’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् divide भारतवर्ष (undivided India) into seven deśas or regions. They are: अपरान्त, मध्यदेश, Udīcya or Uttarāpatha, Prācya, Dākṣiṇātya or दक्षिणापथ, विन्ध्य-pṛṣṭha and Parvata.
The मध्यदेश is defined as that part of the country which is between the हिमालयस् and the विन्ध्य Mountains, but to the west of प्रयाग (modern Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh) and to the east of विनशन (the place where the river सरस्वती disappears).
Seventeen types of people are mentioned in the epics and the पुराणस् as living in this region. Some of them are: कुरु, Pāñcāla, Śālva, Jāṅgala, शूरसेन, Bodha, Kulya, किरात, Magadha and so on. Obviously they seem to be the names of the countries or regions in which they lived.

Madhvācārya
(A. D. 1238-1317)
------------------------------------------
‘Too much is too bad!’—is a popular saying. Excessive intellectualism can lead to a dryness of the heart. Exuberant emotionalism, on the other hand, can generate superstition and fanaticism. It was given to Madhvācārya—also known as पूर्णप्रज्ञ and Ānandatīrtha—to strike a delicate balance between these two extreme positions in इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् as also in the society of his times.
MadhavācāryaThe most authentic source of his life is the famous work Madhvavijaya in Sanskrit by नारायण Paṇḍita (A. D. 1287-1350) who was a junior contemporary of the आचार्य himself. He was the son of त्रिविक्रम Paṇḍita who was an advaitin first but was converted to dvaitism by the आचार्य.
According to the द्वैत tradition, मध्वाचार्य was an इन्चर्नतिओन् of Mukhyaprāṇa (same as हिरण्यगर्भ, also known as वायु and सूत्रात्मन्, an emanation of Lord विष्णु), who had incarnated earlier as Māruti (Hanumān) and भीम (the middle one among the Pāṇdava brothers).
He was born in A. D. 1238 as the son of Madhyageha भट्ट at the village Pājaka or Pājakakṣetra, in the State of Karnataka, near the city of Mangalore. He was given the name ‘Vāsudeva’ during the नामकरण (naming) ceremony. Even as a child he exhibited many miraculous powers like clinging to the tail of a bull which was grazing in bushy fields, for several hours, converting tamarind seeds into gold and giving them to the person to whom his own ड़थेर् was indebted, thus discharging him from his debt, spending several days in the नारायण temple in the forest of Kaḍuvūr all alone, correcting a ब्राह्मण pundit who was reciting the पुराणस् wrongly and so on.
After his उपनयन, he was put under the care of a preceptor. However, वासुदेव spent most of the time in manly sports like running, wrestling and swimming rather than attending the classes. When the teacher objected, he showed him that he knew all that was taught and also where the teacher was wrong!
At the age of sixteen वासुदेव took सṁन्यास दीक्षा (monastic vows) from Acyutaprekṣa, the pontiff of a monastery at Kāre near the modern town of उडुपि. He was given the new name ‘Pūrṇaprajña’.
The new ascetic began to receive instructions in the doctrines of Advaita Vedānta according to the famous work Iṣṭasiddhi of विमुक्तात्मन् (10th century A. D.). However, serious differences cropped up between the teacher and the disciple very soon. Being astounded by the sharp memory and remarkable scholarship of the disciple, Acyutaprekṣa gave him another name ‘Ānandatīrtha’ and also made him the pontiff of his monastery. ‘Madhva or मध्वाचार्य’ seems to be a synonym of his real name. However it is this name that seems to have become more common and popular.
During the next few years, Madhvā-cārya battled with many a scholar—most of whom were arrogant due to their learning—defeated them and converted them to his own views.
He then undertook a पिल्ग्रिमगे of South India. Along with visiting the holy places he also utilised this opportunity for spreading his views on the basic texts of Vedānta. At one of the meetings during this tour, he was challenged by some scholars to explain the scriptures. मध्वाचार्य by the dint of his scholarship and eloquence showed that each Vedic सूक्त had three meanings, the Mahā-bhārata ten, and that each name of the Viṣṇusahasranāma had a hundred!
The confrontation with the scholars of various schools like those of शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) and Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137) convinced him now, of the need to found a new school of thought of Vedānta. During his next trip to North India, he is said to have visited the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, Badarī. There, he proceeded to the inaccessible regions of upper Badarī, met वेदव्यास who lived there with his disciples, invisible to the ordinary run of humanity, and, received his instruction about the true meaning of the Brahma-sūtras as also the Mahābhārata and the Pāñcarātra Āgamas, all of which were composed by him to establish the glory of नारायण. He then wrote his commentary on the Brahmasūtras and travelled back to South India.
During this second sojourn in this part of the country, he won over two great scholars—Śobhana भट्ट of the गोदावरी region and Svāmi Śāstri from Kaliṅga—and gave them सṁन्यास. They were renamed Padmanābha Tīrtha and नरहरि तीर्थ. They, later on, wrote commentaries on मध्वाचार्य’s works.
It was at this time that Acyutaprekṣa (his गुरु) became the disciple of this illustrious disciple.
During the period of his stay at उडुपि, he discovered the image of Śrī कृष्ण which was imbedded in a huge lump of mud (called गोपीचन्दन). He got it washed in a nearby lake and himself carried it to his monastery. It was during this procession that he composed, out of divine inspiration, the now well-known Dvādaśastotra, twelve stanzas on Lord वासुदेव (or Śrī कृष्ण). As per this hymn, this image had been prepared by the divine architect and sculptor विश्वकर्म and that it had been worshipped by the गोपीस् of Vṛndāvana as also the queen रुक्मिणी.
He then got a temple built and installed this image there.
During this period of stay at उडुपि, he reformed the ways of sacrificial rites, introduced the use of animal forms made of a paste of black gram powder and ghee instead of real animals and included them in devotional disciplines.
He went on a second पिल्ग्रिमगे to Badarī during which trip, performed many more miracles like casting a spell on a Turkish Muslim chieftain, routing bands of thieves and robbers, walking effortlessly on the water of the river गङ्गा and throwing away a huge tiger that tried to attack his party. He is also said to have shown the गदा (mace) which he had used in his previous इन्चर्नतिओन् as भीम.
The various miracles attributed to him in the traditional biography (the Madhvavijaya) may be taken to show that the आचार्य was a giant both physically and intellectually as also in yogic powers.
When he was staying at उडुपि, the manuscripts of his works were stolen by rival scholars but were recovered in a miraculous way.
It was during this period that he won over a great scholar—Trivikrama Paṇḍita—after defeating him in a long fought battle of wit and scholarship. At his command, त्रिविक्रम later wrote an elaborate explanatory commentary on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of his गुरु.
Since he was very particular that the worship of Lord कृष्ण in the temple he had established at उडुपि should go on smoothly and unhindered, he gave that responsibility to his eight saṁnyāsin disciples. They established their maṭhas or monasteries round the temple and took turns to shoulder that responsibility, each of the pontiffs getting a two-year term. These eight maṭhas known as ‘Aṣṭamaṭhas’, are Adamāru मठ, Kāṇiyūru मठ, Kṛṣṇāpura मठ, Palimāru मठ, Pejāvara मठ, Puttige मठ, Śīrūru मठ and Sode मठ. The first pontiffs of these Maṭhas, respectively, were: Narasiṁhatīrtha, Vāmanatīrtha, Janārdanatīrtha, Hṛṣīkeśatīrtha, Akṣobhyatīrtha, Upendratīrtha, राम-tīrtha and Viṣṇutīrtha.
Having intuitively felt that he had finished his work, मध्वाचार्य is said to have mysteriously disappeared from his seat, while teaching the Aitareya Upaniṣad to his disciples, leaving a big heap of flowers on it.
As regards the personality of मध्वाचार्य, the Madhvavijaya describes him as very strong with handsome features. He was endowed with a photographic memory, astounding scholarship and a powerful oratory. His voice was sonorous and suited the chanting of Vedic and other mantras.
A vast body of 37 works is attributed to him. Only a few of the more important ones may be mentioned here:
Bhāṣyas on all the ten well-known उपनिषद्स्;
Bhagavadgītābhāṣya; Bhagavadgītā-tātparyanirṇaya; Brahmasūtrabhāṣya; Aṇubhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras; Anu-vyākhyāna, also on the same work; Māyā-vādakhaṇḍana; Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya; Sadācārasmṛti; Yatipraṇavakalpa; Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya; Dvādaśa-stotra and Ṛgvedabhāṣya (first मण्डल’s forty sūktas only).
Madhvācārya advocated dualism and realism. His philosophy accepts pañca-bhedas or five kinds of bhedas (differences) which are real and permanent. They are: ईश्वर or God is different from the jīvas or souls; he is also different from the jaḍa (insentient nature, प्रकृति); the various jīvas are different from one another; the jīvas are different from the jaḍa; the various objects which are jaḍa, are also different from one another.
He accepts God, called नारायण or विष्णु or Śrīhari, as the Supreme Reality and the others as dependent realities. मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्, which is regaining one’s blissful nature, can be got only through भक्ति or devotion to God.
The illustrious successors of Madhvā-cārya like जयतीर्थ (circa A. D. 1250) and Vyāsarāya (A. D. 1478-1539) as also राघवेन्द्रतीर्थ (A. D. 1595-1671) have kept up the द्वैत Vedānta philosophy alive. The saints of the दासकूट (See DĀSAKŪṬA for details.) have nourished the tradition of भक्ति or devotion to God as कृष्ण (Nārāyaṇa or विष्णु).
The contribution of मध्वाचार्य to Hindu philosophy and to the cult of भक्ति is remarkable.
See also DVAITA-VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA.

madhuparka
(‘offering mixed with honey’)
------------------------------------------
An अतिथि or a guest has to be treated as if he is a god. Thus states the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.11).
Honouring guests and elders as also holy persons has been a bounden duty, especially for the गृहस्थ or the householder.
Madhuparka is an important item offered to such guests. It may be prepared out of three materials (curds, honey and ghee) or five (curds, honey, ghee, water and ground grain or sugar).
In the earliest days, flesh was one of these five items, but seems to have been given up later when ड़्लेस्ह्-एअतिन्ग् came to be abhorred.
The persons to whom मधुपर्क has to be offered, especially when they come to one’s होउसे, are: ऋत्विक् (Vedic priest), आचार्य (preceptor), bride-groom (during मर्रिअगे), स्नातक (a student of Vedic studies who has just graduated) and a king.
Elaborate rules have been given in the smṛtis as to the mode of offering मधुपर्क and also in receiving and consuming it (vide आश्वलायन Gṛhya-sūtras 1.24.5-26).
The Kauśikasūtras (92) dealing with the gṛhya rites mentions nine kinds of mixtures as fit to be offered like मधुपर्क.
For instance the brāhma mixture has honey and curds; the aindra, pāyasa (pudding) only; saumya, curds and ghee; vāruṇa, water and ghee and so on. These mixtures seem to be offered during certain वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् like राजसूय and Sautrāmaṇi.

Madhusūdana Sarasvatī
(A. D. 1490-1580)
------------------------------------------
Rare are the savants who have simultaneously enriched the literature on Advaita Vedānta and भक्ति or devotion to personal God. मधुसूदन सरस्वती was certainly an outstanding one among them.
Research scholars assign to him three dates: A. D. 1490-1580; A. D. 1525-1632 and A. D. 1490-1607.
He was the third son of Pramodana Purandarācārya of Bengal, born probably at Unaśiyā in the district Faridpur, now in Bangladesh. His ancestors are said to have migrated from Kanauj in Uttar Pradesh.
As a boy, Madhusūdana was a brilliant student and learnt Sanskrit grammar and poetry at the feet of his own ड़थेर्, who himself was a great scholar.
He is believed to have renounced the world at the age of ten and travelled all the way to नवद्वीप (in West Bengal) to meet Śrī कृष्ण चैतन्य, known widely as चैतन्य महाप्रभु. Since चैतन्य was away, he stayed on there itself and pursued his studies of न्याय philosophy under Mathurānātha Tarkavāgīśa, who was the foremost scholar of his times in that field.
He then proceeded to काशी to learn Advaita Vedānta under रामतीर्थ and then the Mīmāṁsā philosophy under a saṁnyāsin, Mādhava सरस्वती. These studies produced an intense spirit of renunciation in him so much so that he took सṁन्यास from Viśveśvara सरस्वती.
He is credited with the organising of a sect of militant मोन्क्स्, the Nāgā साधुस्, in order to protect the Hindu saṁnyāsins and other Hindus.
He had three eminent disciples: बल-bhadra Bhaṭṭācārya, Śeṣagovinda and पुरुषोत्तम सरस्वती.
He authored six important works. They are: Vedāntakalpalatikā, Siddhānta-bindu, Bhaktirasāyana, Advaitasiddhi, Saṅkṣepaśārīrakavyākhyā, Bhāgavataṭīkā and Gūḍhārthadīpikā.
Total number of works attributed to him are eighteen.
The Advaitasiddhi is his magnum opus. The Gūḍhārthadīpikā is a lucid gloss on शङ्कर’s commentary of the Bhagavadgītā. The Siddhāntabindu is a scholarly commentary on the Daśaślokī of शङ्कर. The Bhaktirasāyana is a well-organised treatise on भक्ति or devotion to God.
See also ADVAITASIDDHI.

madhurabhāva
(‘the sweet attitude’)
------------------------------------------
There is an innate hankering in every सोउल् for enjoying infinite bliss. Though all the four yogas recognise this, it is भक्ति-योग that gives us a more practical mode of sādhana or spiritual discipline, to attain this.
It is easier for a human being who is strongly encased in the body-मिन्द् complex and hence terribly attached to it, to contemplate on God with a form, a name and a personality of his own. The Hindu scriptures including the उपनिषद्स् describe God, not only as Sat (the eternal) but also as आनन्द (infinite bliss). He is also ‘Sundara’ (the Beautiful) as per the description in the Viṣṇusahasranāma (no. 791) which is a part of the Mahābhārata. Hence he is the fittest person to be loved.
Bhaktiyoga teaches several modes of loving God, of which मधुरभाव or madhurabhakti is also one. It is the love that makes the devotee look upon God as one’s beloved and long for union with him. It is this kind of love that the गोपीस् (cowherdesses) of Vṛndāvana of म्य्थोलोग्य् or आण्डाऌ (one of the आऌवार्स् who was a woman) (circa 8th century A. D.), अक्क महादेवी (d. A. D. 1166) and Mīrā (A. D. 1450-1547) of the historical period practised in their lives, loving God as their husband or beloved.
Madhurabhāva concedes that sensual love is a perverted form of divine love, and, if directed towards God, can transmute काम (lust) into prema (divine love).
See also BHAKTA, BHAKTI and BHAKTI-YOGA.

Madhu
------------------------------------------
Viṣṇu is often described as the enemy of मधु and कैटभ, two powerful demons. These demons were brothers. They emerged out of the ears of विष्णु when he was sleeping and threatened to kill ब्रह्मा. ब्रह्मा prayed to मोथेर् Kālī, the presiding deity of विष्णु’s sleep. After she emerged out of विष्णु’s body, he woke up from his sleep and killed the two demons with his discus. There was another demon मधु, the son of the demoness Lolā and ड़थेर् of Lavaṇāsura. He was a great devotee of शिव and had obtained a powerful trident from him, on the condition that he should never use it against the देवस् or gods, nor harm the people of the world. He built a city called Madhupura (or मधुरा) and was ruling there. His queen was Kumbhīnasī. When his son Lavaṇāsura started transgressing धर्म, he became disgusted, gave the trident to him and went away for तपस् or practising austerities.
Lavaṇāsura was later killed by शत्रुघ्न, younger brother of राम.
